claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9457 s3: "The canonical model for problem details is a JSON object... that format is identified with the \"application/problem+json\" media type." s3.1 lists exactly five members (type, status, title, detail, instance); s3.2: "Problem type definitions MAY extend the problem details object with additional members that are specific to that problem type." s1: "problem details are (naturally) not the only way to convey the details of a problem in HTTP". Ledger text now equals round-1 suggested_text; lesson s3 now says "this lesson uses four of its fields".

RFC 9457 s3.1.1: "When this member is not present, its value is assumed to be \"about:blank\"." s4.2.1: the "about:blank" URI "indicates that the problem has no additional semantics beyond that of the HTTP status code." Unchanged since round 1.

RFC 9457 s3.1.2: "The \"status\" member is a JSON number indicating the HTTP status code generated by the origin server for this occurrence of the problem." and "The \"status\" member, if present, is only advisory; it conveys the HTTP status code used for the convenience of the consumer. Generators MUST use the same status code in the actual HTTP response." The round-1 gap is closed: lesson s4 now says "The status line is still the authoritative one; the body's copy is there for code that kept only the parsed body".

RFC 9457 s1: "Problem details can be used with any HTTP status code, but they most naturally fit the semantics of 4xx and 5xx responses." Worked examples in s3 use 403 Forbidden and 422 Unprocessable Content, both client errors. Ledger text now equals round-1 suggested_text (the earlier "403 and 503" error is gone).

Re-ran `curl -sS -i http://localhost:8080/conflict` this session against the running lab:
HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Server: Caddy
Content-Length: 37

Conflict: this order was already paid
Matches the claim and the lesson's "Expected result" on status, Content-Type, length, exact body, no JSON, no error field. `version_key: caddy` now present.

RFC 9457 s3.1.1: "The \"type\" member is a JSON string containing a URI reference that identifies the problem type." "Consumers MUST use the \"type\" URI (after resolution, if necessary) as the problem type's primary identifier." "it is RECOMMENDED that absolute URIs be used in \"type\" when possible". The lesson's "not as an address the client fetches" is backed by: "consumers SHOULD NOT automatically dereference the type URI, unless they do so when providing information to developers." "not a plain sentence" follows from URI-reference syntax (no spaces).

RFC 9457 s3.1.3: "The \"title\" member is a JSON string containing a short, human-readable summary of the problem type." "It SHOULD NOT change from occurrence to occurrence of the problem, except for localization." s3.1.4: "The \"detail\" member is a JSON string containing a human-readable explanation specific to this occurrence of the problem." Lesson s3 hedges correctly ("meant to read the same on every occurrence"); s4's "stay fixed" drops the localization exception, which the ledger keeps — acceptable at this level, not raised as an issue.

Grepped the local mirror refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt. s15.5.1: "The 400 (Bad Request) status code indicates that the server cannot or will not process the request due to something that is perceived to be a client error (e.g., malformed request syntax, invalid request message framing, or deceptive request routing)." s15.5.5: "...the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource or is not willing to disclose that one exists." s15.5.10: "...the request could not be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the target resource." Ledger wording matches all three.

issues.quote: the response's first line, where the status code always travels, outside the body
issues.text: True of HTTP/1.1 only. RFC 9112 s4 defines `status-line = HTTP-version SP status-code SP [ reason-phrase ]` as the first line of a response; RFC 9110 (the `http` version_key here) never uses the term and treats the status code as control data. Over HTTP/2/3 the code travels in a `:status` pseudo-header field, so "always" is false there. The lab is HTTP/1.1 (`curl -i http://localhost:8080/conflict` → `HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict`), so nothing a junior sees contradicts it — hence minor, not major.
issues.fix: Drop the absolute: "...already on the response's status line — the first line of an HTTP/1.1 response, where the status code travels, outside the body — repeated inside the body."

issues.quote: A `400` still means the request itself was malformed or failed validation
issues.text: RFC 9110 s15.5.1 gives only "something that is perceived to be a client error (e.g., malformed request syntax, invalid request message framing, or deceptive request routing)" — validation failure is nowhere in the definition, and RFC 9110 s15.5.21 defines 422 for content whose syntax is correct "but was unable to process the contained instructions" (RFC 9457's own worked example uses 422). Claim 10 says "malformed or otherwise invalid", which is fine; the lesson's "failed validation" is stronger than its own claim and pre-empts backend.l1.choosing-an-error-status.
issues.fix: Write: "A `400` still means the server treats the request itself as the client's mistake". Leave which code a validation failure gets to backend.l1.validating-input / backend.l1.choosing-an-error-status.

issues.quote: fixed responses from Caddy (a web server) stood in for a real API ... the blocks below are from that file
issues.text: "that file" has no antecedent: the sentence names Caddy the program, never a config file, so the demonstrative points at nothing in the prose (the filename only exists in the fence meta `file=Caddyfile`, which the reader may not see). Content is correct — `git show stage-0:Caddyfile` is the source of both blocks.
issues.fix: Name it once: "...fixed responses from Caddy (a web server) stood in for a real API, configured in a file called the Caddyfile ... the blocks below are from that file".

issues.quote: a later stage replaced that fixed body with a real endpoint, and what it answers now is a different lesson's subject
issues.text: Unlisted claim about the example repo's later state, added in the round-1 junior fix without a ledger entry. I verified it myself, so it is not an accuracy risk (hence minor, not major per Step 1): at HEAD (post stage-1) the Caddyfile has no `@missingOrder` handler and instead carries `handle /api/v1/* { reverse_proxy api:8080 }`, while `handle /conflict` is byte-identical to stage-0 — which also validates s2's present tense "/conflict already answers 409".
issues.fix: Add a claim (kind `fact`, no version_key, source_hint "examples/don-hang @ HEAD: Caddyfile handle /api/v1/* → reverse_proxy api:8080; /conflict unchanged since stage-0") covering both the s7 warning and s5's "`@missingOrder` is the name this file gives to requests for `/api/v1/orders/999`" (Caddyfile:30 at stage-0).

issues.quote: `title` is also meant to be a short summary rather than a URI, so moving the text there wouldn't fix the actual issue
issues.text: Key `a` is correct and b/c/d are wrong as asked ("What's the issue with this choice?" — the issue is the value's shape, not which field). But d's explanation argues against itself: "`title` is also meant to be a short summary rather than a URI" is a reason why "order not found" WOULD sit fine in `title` (RFC 9457 s3.1.3: "a short, human-readable summary of the problem type"), so the sentence reads as support for d rather than a refutation.
issues.fix: Rewrite d's explanation: "Moving the text to `title` would be a fine second step — \"order not found\" is exactly a title — but it doesn't answer what's wrong here: `type` would still be holding a value that isn't a URI reference, or be missing entirely."

issues.quote: RFC 9457 defines one more field, `instance`, and lets an API add fields of its own
issues.text: I am given a fifth field's name and nothing else — not what goes in it, not why I am not learning it. The paragraph's job is to tell me the four fields are not the whole story, and it does, but `instance` leaves an open question I cannot close from the text, and I spent a moment checking whether I would need it for the quiz (I do not; nothing asks).
issues.fix: Either give `instance` a half-line of meaning in the same sentence, or write "defines one more field this lesson doesn't use" without naming it.

issues.quote: the same HTTP status code already on the response's status line, the first line of an HTTP/1.1 response, where the status code travels outside the body — repeated inside the body
issues.text: I read this bullet three times. Two definitions are stacked before the sentence gets back to its own point: "status line" is explained by an appositive, that appositive then gets its own "where…" clause, and only after the dash does the sentence return to the field. On my first pass I attached "repeated inside the body" to the nearest words and got nonsense.
issues.fix: Split it in two: "`status` — the same HTTP status code already on the response's status line, repeated inside the body. The status line is the first line of an HTTP/1.1 response, so that number normally travels outside the body."

issues.quote: the first line of an HTTP/1.1 response
issues.text: This is the only version number in the lesson and it is never tied to anything I can see. Stated that precisely, it reads as a warning that somewhere else things differ — is there a version of HTTP where the status code is not on the first line, and is the lab even speaking 1.1? Neither the lesson nor the prerequisites tells me, so I cannot decide whether this matters to me.
issues.fix: Tie it to what Try it shows: "the first line of an HTTP/1.1 response — the version you'll see in the `curl -i` output".

issues.quote: a `404` still means the server has no current representation for that resource
issues.text: "Representation" is new to me and it is doing real work: I do know "resource", so "no current representation for that resource" sounds like the resource exists but something else about it is missing. I read the phrase in its everyday sense and moved on, without being able to tell whether it is a technical term I should have been taught. The two neighbouring clauses in the same sentence ("malformed", "a conflict with the resource's current state") use only words I already have.
issues.fix: Match the neighbours' register: "a `404` still means the server has nothing to return for that resource".

issues.quote: Problem Details body: type, title, status, detail
issues.text: By the end I have never seen the four fields together in one body. I know what each field is for and the diagram lists the names, but the lesson is titled "one shape for every error" and that shape is the one thing never shown — while both of the ad-hoc shapes it replaces are quoted in full in section 5. When quiz q6 showed me `"type": "order not found"`, I was imagining the surrounding object for the first time.
issues.fix: Add one prose sentence after the `detail` bullet saying what the four fields would hold for the stage-0 missing order: a URL-shaped name in `type`, a fixed summary in `title`, `404` in `status`, and the missing order's id in `detail`.

issues.quote: a later stage replaced that fixed body with a real endpoint
issues.text: Section 5 introduces both blocks as stage-0 ("At stage-0, fixed responses from Caddy … stood in for a real API"), and Try it then tells me one of the two no longer runs. So when I am asked to curl `/conflict` and expect exactly the quoted plain text, I cannot tell from the text whether that second block is still the one answering me today or whether a later stage changed it too. I only find out by running it.
issues.fix: In Try it step 1, add a clause: "run `curl -sS -i http://localhost:8080/conflict` — unlike the handler above, this one is still exactly the block quoted in section 5".

issues.text: I can copy the command, but I do not know what `-sS -i` do. The Expected result asks me to check a `409` and a `Content-Type` header, and those are exactly what `-i` makes visible. If I had typed the shorter `curl <url>` I have seen elsewhere, I would see only the plain-text line, miss both things I am told to check, and think I had done it wrong.
issues.fix: Name the flag's job in the same step: "(`-i` prints the status line and headers, not just the body)".

issues.quote: False, because plain-text errors like `/conflict` aren't exempt either — Problem Details is exactly what replaces them.

issues.quote: Only the shape of the body — it still returns `404`, now with `type`/`title`/`status`/`detail` fields instead of the ad-hoc `error` field
